extracted.intended_audience: college/university faculty, curriculum developers, and assessment staff interested in quantitative literacy (QL) programs
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and criteria for designing, implementing, and evaluating quantitative-literacy (QL) curricula and assessments across the college curriculum, including program goals, course-level evaluation, faculty development, and survey-based measurement of student attitudes and skills.

rubrics_metrics.name: Quantitative-intensive course evaluation form
rubrics_metrics.description: At the completion of all quantitative-intensive courses, students are asked to report on the types of quantitative work they did, evaluate opportunities to develop quantitative reasoning and the usefulness of feedback on quantitative work, and provide self-reports of changes in their quantitative reasoning skills.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This form was used as an initial assessment step and collected student perception data across seven terms; a subset of questions was incorporated into every course evaluation to make student perceptions a continuing part of the general education assessment plan.

rubrics_metrics.name: Assessment instrument — foundational mathematical and statistical skills
rubrics_metrics.description: One component of the proposed QL assessment instrument is measurement of foundational mathematical and statistical skills.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Intended to capture basic computational and procedural competencies that underlie further quantitative reasoning; to be used alongside discipline-specific measures.

rubrics_metrics.name: Assessment instrument — quantitative reasoning skills (general and discipline-specific)
rubrics_metrics.description: The assessment instrument should measure quantitative reasoning skills both in a general sense and as they appear within particular disciplines.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use of both general QL items and discipline-specific tasks will permit analysis of transfer of skills across contexts and the contribution of disciplinary training to overall QL.

rubrics_metrics.name: Assessment instrument — attitudes and beliefs about mathematics and QL
rubrics_metrics.description: Measure students' attitudes and beliefs about mathematics and quantitative literacy as part of a comprehensive QL assessment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Includes items on anxiety, interest in further study, perceived utility of math/statistics; example instrument: Dartmouth 'Mathematics Across the Curriculum' attitudinal survey.

rubrics_metrics.name: Transfer of quantitative skills across contexts
rubrics_metrics.description: A core criterion is whether students can transfer quantitative reasoning skills to new contexts; reinforcement and opportunities to practice throughout the curriculum are necessary to build transfer.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assessment should examine transfer explicitly (e.g., discipline-specific and general measures combined); program design should provide repeated practice in varied contexts to support transfer.

rubrics_metrics.name: Developmental progression: identifying vs generating quantitative reasoning
rubrics_metrics.description: Assess both students' ability to identify sound quantitative arguments and their ability to generate such reasoning independently, recognizing these may develop at different rates.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Research (e.g., in statistics education) suggests students may identify correct reasoning before they can generate it; include items targeting both identification and production of sound quantitative arguments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Confidence with mathematics (math confidence metric)
rubrics_metrics.description: Measure students' confidence and anxiety about mathematics as part of QL assessment (referred to as 'confidence with mathematics').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use pre/post attitudinal instruments (e.g., Dartmouth survey). Tracking confidence changes can indicate program impact on affective barriers to learning QL.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pedagogical practices: feedback, explicit instruction, and explaining reasoning
rubrics_metrics.description: Courses should provide explicit instruction in quantitative skills, useful feedback on quantitative work, and frequent opportunities for students to explain the reasoning behind their work.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Student reports showed higher means for feedback/explicit instruction; upper-level courses asked for explanations more often (possibly due to smaller class size). Encouraging explanation of reasoning at all course levels is identified as an area for improvement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Assessment schedule and procedures (every-five-years review)
rubrics_metrics.description: Conduct a more thorough assessment of the quantitative requirement every five years, with instructors asked to incorporate the assessment instrument into course requirements and additional data collected from outgoing seniors.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Routine cyclical assessment supports long-term program evaluation; embedding instruments in course requirements increases participation and data quality.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use discipline-specific measures with a general QL instrument
rubrics_metrics.description: Combine discipline-specific measures of quantitative reasoning with a general QL instrument to explore transfer and the contribution of disciplinary training.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This combination allows identification of strengths/weaknesses across majors and helps determine whether discipline-specific training meets program QL goals.

rubrics_metrics.name: Faculty development: multidisciplinary discussions and shared language
rubrics_metrics.description: Promote multidisciplinary discussions of appropriate QL goals and create a shared language for talking about quantitative concepts to increase faculty comfort and consistency.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Faculty across disciplines often use different surface presentations of statistical concepts (e.g., significance testing, measurement error); shared language and agreed-upon goals help students see parallels across courses and support transfer.

rubrics_metrics.name: Faculty leadership and modeling metacognitive problem-solving
rubrics_metrics.description: Leadership by faculty comfortable with teaching quantitative reasoning is important; effective models make reasoning explicit and demonstrate metacognitive problem-solving (showing how they stumble and work through challenges).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Modeling explicit reasoning clarifies processes, teaches students to avoid reasoning biases, and provides exemplars for non-math faculty.

rubrics_metrics.name: Program supports: course development grants and co-teaching
rubrics_metrics.description: Provide resources such as course development grants and support for co-teaching to enable cross-disciplinary quantitative-intensive courses.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Funding (e.g., Mellon grants) was used to provide development grants; co-teaching allows cross-disciplinary teams to offer courses like 'quantitative concepts in art' but scheduling and faculty time remain challenges.

rubrics_metrics.name: MAC project goals (1): 'Support faculty in creating projects and/or courses that make the mathematical dimensions of their disciplines more explicit.'
rubrics_metrics.description: Explicit goal from the MAC project focused on enabling faculty to reveal and teach the mathematical aspects of their disciplines.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Supports curriculum reform at faculty level; may be achieved via workshops, mentorship, and institute activities.

rubrics_metrics.name: MAC project goals (2): 'Support faculty in choosing the degree to which they want to infuse math into their curricula.'
rubrics_metrics.description: Allow faculty autonomy in selecting depth/extent of math infusion appropriate to their courses and institutional culture.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognizes varied comfort levels and curricular constraints; provides flexible models from single assignments to full coordinated studies.

rubrics_metrics.name: MAC project goals (3): 'Provide students with experiences that demonstrate the utility, beauty and value of mathematics in their studies and everyday lives.'
rubrics_metrics.description: Design student experiences that communicate both practical utility and aesthetic/value aspects of mathematics.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use applications relevant to students' disciplines and lives to foster engagement and perceived relevance.

rubrics_metrics.name: MAC project goals (4): 'Make mathematics welcome and indispensable across the entire curriculum.'
rubrics_metrics.description: Foster a curricular culture where mathematics is regarded as essential and integrated across disciplines.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Analogous to writing- or speaking-across-the-curriculum initiatives; requires cross-disciplinary commitment.

rubrics_metrics.name: MAC project goals (5): 'Make the methods and materials designed to further the above goals available, accessible, and friendly to the broad national audience of faculty in undergraduate institutions.'
rubrics_metrics.description: Disseminate accessible pedagogy and materials broadly so other faculty can adopt QL approaches.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provide web resources, exemplar curriculum materials, and supportive documentation.

rubrics_metrics.name: MAC project goals (6): 'Collaborate with other projects or initiatives in Washington State concerned with promoting mathematics across the curriculum and improving quantitative or symbolic reasoning or numeracy.'
rubrics_metrics.description: Coordinate with other initiatives to align efforts and share resources for broader impact.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Partnerships expand reach and reduce duplication of effort; example partners include state boards and centers for teaching and learning.

rubrics_metrics.name: Summer Institute structure and expectations
rubrics_metrics.description: Four-day, three-night workshops (MAC Summer Institutes) that provide time/resources for participants to adapt or create projects/courses incorporating mathematics; participants encouraged to attend in interdisciplinary teams and bring a 'math mentor.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Includes sessions on statistics, ethnomathematics, Excel, establishing learning communities, quantitative assessment; provides reference library and networked computers for project work; interdisciplinary teams foster local support networks.

rubrics_metrics.name: Curriculum models for infusion: single assignment
rubrics_metrics.description: A minimal MAC project can be a single assignment or a one-time guest lecture (e.g., a math mentor lecture on graphical ethics followed by application in a writing assignment).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Low barrier to entry; can be implemented with or without a math instructor and threaded through future assignments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Curriculum models for infusion: one- or two-credit math support
rubrics_metrics.description: Add one or two credits of math support to a traditional non-math course, taught alongside the content instructor or during a corresponding time period.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Supports students with weaker math backgrounds; examples include pairing art history with 'Topics in Math' or combining math support with English for Academic Purposes for ESL students.

rubrics_metrics.name: Curriculum models for infusion: large-scale coordinated courses
rubrics_metrics.description: Create entirely new courses or coordinated studies (multiple linked courses, co-teaching) where math and another discipline are integrated over many credits.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: 'Statistical Methods for Sociology', 'Math the Write Way' (intermediate algebra + essay writing), coordinated physics/algebra courses; requires administrative structure and greater faculty commitment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Program assessment methods: counts, student attitudinal surveys, faculty surveys
rubrics_metrics.description: Evaluate the program via (1) facts and figures on involvement (faculty, students, disciplines, institutions), (2) student attitudinal surveys (pre/post administration), and (3) faculty surveys.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Collect demographic/tracking data alongside attitude items; use pre/post designs to detect changes although causation cannot always be established.

rubrics_metrics.name: Dartmouth attitudinal survey (MATC) — content and administration
rubrics_metrics.description: A 51-item attitudinal instrument (35 items from Dartmouth focusing on mathematics + 16 reworded for statistics) covering anxiety/concern about competency, interest in pursuing further study, and perception of practical utility; administered at beginning and end of quarter.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Likert-scale items (1 = Strongly Agree to 5 = Strongly Disagree). Example items showing small positive effect sizes include 'To understand math I sometimes think about my personal experiences', 'I am good at math', 'Math helps me understand the world around me', and 'Writing about mathematics makes it easier to learn.' Analyze overall and subgroup (e.g., gender) differences.
